title: Expect tests: tests that show their output
body: An expect test prints values and records the output next to the code. With `ppx_expect` you write `let%expect_test "name" = print_endline (f x); [%expect {| result |}]`, and `dune test` fails if the real output differs. The expected text is part of the source, so a reviewer sees behaviour and test together.

When output legitimately changes, run `dune promote` and Dune rewrites the expected blocks to match; you then review the diff in version control. That workflow makes exploratory testing cheap, which is why Jane Street uses it widely, but the promotion step is a review step, not a rubber stamp.

Enable the tests by adding `(inline_tests)` and `(preprocess (pps ppx_expect))` to a library stanza. Keep tests deterministic: avoid timestamps, hash-table iteration order and absolute paths in the printed output.
challenge: The tests in test/slug_tests.ml fail because `Slug.slugify` returns its input unchanged. Implement it so it lowercases letters and digits, turns every run of other characters into one hyphen, and never starts or ends with a hyphen.
projectInstructions: Run `dune test --root .` to see the failing expectations. Edit only src/slug.ml. When all three tests pass, try changing a hyphen to an underscore to watch the test fail.
question: What does `dune promote` do after an expect test fails?
correct: It rewrites the expected blocks in the source to match the actual output, which you then review
wrong: It re-runs the tests with a longer timeout
reasoning: Expect tests store output in the source, so promotion updates those blocks; the human step is reviewing the resulting diff.
